Cymraeg

Y Brenin a Fu ac a Fydd

Llys Cynyr, draig fach, a'r bachgen a fydd yn frenin

40 chapters, with exercises; answers at the end. Text status: 40 chapters draft. Interactive version: https://charlesr-w.github.io/illustrated-input/?course=cy-brenin-01.

How to read this book

This book teaches Welsh the way Lingua Latina per se Illustrata teaches Latin: by reading one continuous story written entirely in Welsh, from the first page.

Read for meaning, not for every word. Each chapter adds only a little new language, and the story, the pictures and what you already know are meant to make it clear. If a sentence is unclear, read on: the next sentence often answers it.

Use the margin. The notes beside the text are in Welsh only. "mawr ↔ bach" means opposites. "=" gives a simpler way of saying the same thing. "gadair ← cadair" shows the ordinary form of a word whose first letter has changed (a mutation). A small picture shows an object.

Re-read. When a chapter feels easy, read it again with the notes hidden. A second, faster reading is where much of the learning happens.

Do the Pensa, ideally aloud. A practises the chapter's grammar, B its new words, C asks questions about the story. Each starts with a worked example. Nothing is locked behind a score: check, show the answer, or move on.

Export the Anki cards for each chapter you finish (or all chapters so far) and review them daily. The cards show the Welsh word with an example sentence from the story.

The Welsh is southern Welsh, as taught by the national Learn Welsh courses.

Please note: all chapters are drafts. They were written with AI assistance and have not yet been checked by a fluent Welsh speaker. Corrections are welcome.

Rhan 1 · Pennod 1

Ynys Prydain

I. Ynys Prydain

Dyma'r map. Dyma Ynys Prydain, ar y map. Dyma Iwerddon, ar y map hefyd. Mae Ynys Prydain yn Ewrop. Mae Iwerddon yn Ewrop hefyd.

dyma'r = dyma + y · Ble? → yn Ewrop

Ble mae Cymru? Yn Ynys Prydain. Ble mae Lloegr? Yn Ynys Prydain hefyd. Ac mae'r Alban yn Ynys Prydain. Cymru, Lloegr a'r Alban: dyma Ynys Prydain.

Dyma'r môr: môr mawr. Mae Ynys Prydain ac Iwerddon yn y môr. Mae Ynys Prydain yn fawr: mae Ynys Prydain yn ynys fawr iawn.

fawr ← mawr · yn Ewrop · yn fawr

Mae Cymru'n wlad, ac mae Lloegr yn wlad hefyd. Ond mae Cymru'n wlad fach, ac mae Lloegr yn wlad fawr. A'r Alban? Mae'r Alban yn wlad fawr hefyd.

wlad ← gwlad (b.) · fach ← bach · fach bach ↔ mawr

Mae môr mawr rhwng Ynys Prydain ac Iwerddon. Ble mae Iwerddon? Yn y môr, wrth Ynys Prydain. Mae Iwerddon yn ynys hefyd, ac mae Iwerddon yn wlad. Mae Iwerddon yn fawr, ond mae Ynys Prydain yn fawr iawn. Ac mae Cymru rhwng Iwerddon a Lloegr.

Ble mae Llydaw? Mae Llydaw yn Ewrop, ac mae môr rhwng Llydaw a Lloegr. Mae Llydaw yn wlad fach. Mae Ynys Prydain yn fawr, ond mae'r môr yn fawr iawn.

fach ← bach

II. Mynyddoedd ac afonydd

Dyma Gymru. Mae Cymru'n fach, ond mae mynyddoedd mawr yng Nghymru. Ble mae'r mynyddoedd uchel? Yn Eryri. Dyma Eryri, a dyma'r Wyddfa. Mae'r Wyddfa'n fynydd uchel iawn. Mae mynyddoedd uchel yn yr Alban hefyd.

Gymru ← Cymru · mynydd ▲, mynyddoedd ▲▲ · yng Nghymru ← yn + Cymru · fynydd ← mynydd

Ble mae Ynys Môn? Yn y môr, wrth Eryri. Mae Ynys Môn yn ynys fach, ac mae Ynys Môn yng Nghymru.

Mae afonydd yng Nghymru hefyd. Dyma Afon Hafren. Mae Hafren yn afon hir iawn, ac mae Hafren yng Nghymru ac yn Lloegr. Dyma Afon Wysg. Ble mae Afon Wysg? Yng Nghymru. Mae Afon Wysg yn hir, ond mae Hafren yn hir iawn.

afon, afonydd

Ble mae Caerllion? Mae Caerllion yng Nghymru, wrth Afon Wysg. Mae Caerllion yn ddinas. Dyma'r ddinas: mae waliau hir ac uchel yn y ddinas.

ddinas ← dinas (b.) · dinas · y ddinas ← dinas (b.)

Mae trefi yng Nghymru hefyd. Mae Caerfyrddin yn dref. Ond mae'r trefi'n fach, ac mae'r ddinas yn fawr. Ble mae Llundain? Yn Lloegr. Mae Llundain yn ddinas fawr iawn.

tref, trefi · tref · dref ← tref (b.) · trefi'n = trefi yn

III. Cwm Helyg

Ble mae Cwm Helyg ar y map? Yng Nghymru, rhwng y mynyddoedd. Mae Cwm Helyg yn fach iawn ar y map! Ond dyma'r cwm: Cwm Helyg. Mae mynyddoedd tywyll wrth y cwm.

tywyll

Mae'r cwm yn hir, ac mae afon yn y cwm: Afon Helyg. Mae Hafren yn afon fawr, ond mae Afon Helyg yn afon fach. Ac wrth yr afon? Tref fach.

Mae coedwig yn y cwm hefyd, ac mae'r goedwig yn fawr ac yn dywyll. Mae'r goedwig wrth yr afon.

y goedwig ← coedwig (b.) · dywyll ← tywyll

Mae bryn uchel wrth y goedwig. Ond mae'r mynyddoedd yn uchel iawn. Ar y bryn? Ogof. Mae'r ogof yn uchel ar y bryn. Mae'r ogof yn fawr, ac mae'r ogof yn dywyll iawn.

bryn = mynydd bach · ogof · yn + uchel → yn uchel · yn y cwm (Ble?) ↔ yn fawr · dywyll ← tywyll

Ble mae Llys Cynyr? Yng Nghwm Helyg, wrth yr afon. Dyma'r llys: Llys Cynyr. Mae wal hir wrth y llys. Mae tŷ mawr yn y llys, ac mae tai yn y llys hefyd. Mae'r tŷ mawr yn hir, ac mae'r tai'n fach. Ble mae'r goedwig dywyll? Rhwng y llys a'r bryn.

yng Nghwm ← yn + Cwm · tŷ · tai

Mae'r llys yn y cwm. Mae'r cwm yng Nghymru. Ac mae Cymru yn Ynys Prydain, ar y map.

Ac yn y tŷ mawr? Teulu: teulu mawr. Mae teulu mawr yn y llys.

teulu

Nodyn (Saesneg)

The main sentence pattern in this chapter is Mae + subject + yn + …. A Welsh sentence usually begins with its verb. Mae is a form of bod ('to be') meaning 'is' or 'are'; after it comes the subject (the person or thing the sentence is about): Mae Ynys Prydain yn Ewrop ('The island of Britain is in Europe'). Mae can also introduce something, where English says 'there is' or 'there are': Mae afonydd yng Nghymru hefyd ('There are rivers in Wales too'). Here afonydd is indefinite: 'rivers', not 'the rivers'. Welsh has no word for 'a'. 'The' has three forms: 'r after a word ending in a vowel; otherwise yr before a vowel or h-, and y before other consonants: Dyma'r map ('Here is the map').

Yn does two different jobs, and the table 'yn Ewrop ↔ yn fawr' sets them side by side. The first yn means 'in'. It is a preposition: a small word before a noun that shows place, like ar 'on', wrth 'by' and rhwng 'between'. These answer Ble? ('Where?'): Mae Caerllion yng Nghymru, wrth Afon Wysg ('Caerllion is in Wales, by the river Wysg'). An answer can be just the place phrase: Ble mae Iwerddon? Yn y môr, wrth Ynys Prydain ('Where is Ireland? In the sea, by the island of Britain'), or even one noun: Ar y bryn? Ogof. ('On the hill? A cave.')

Yn 'in' is written in full, even after a vowel: Mae Cymru yn Ynys Prydain ('Wales is in the island of Britain'). With Cymru and Cwm Helyg it changes shape, and so does the next word: yng Nghymru ('in Wales'), Yng Nghwm Helyg ('In Cwm Helyg'). This is called nasal mutation. Take these two as fixed chunks for now; the Treigladau table points to Pennod 16 for it.

The second yn links the subject to its predicate: the part of the sentence that says what the subject is or what it is like. After this yn comes an adjective (a describing word, such as mawr 'big') or a noun: Mae Ynys Prydain yn fawr ('The island of Britain is big'), Mae Caerllion yn ddinas ('Caerllion is a city'). English just says 'is'. After a vowel this yn is written 'n: Mae Cymru'n wlad ('Wales is a country'). Iawn 'very' follows the adjective: Mae'r ogof yn fawr, ac mae'r ogof yn dywyll iawn ('The cave is big, and the cave is very dark'). To tell the two kinds of yn apart, ask Ble?: yn Ewrop answers it, yn fawr does not.

This second yn also changes the first letter of the next word. Regular sound changes like this are called mutations (treigladau); this one is soft mutation, the commonest. The rule line gives it: m → f, b → f, g drops, d → dd, t → d, c → g, p → b. So mynydd gives Mae'r Wyddfa'n fynydd uchel iawn ('Yr Wyddfa is a very high mountain'), bach gives Mae Cymru'n fach ('Wales is small'), and likewise gwlad → yn wlad ('a country'), dinas → yn ddinas ('a city'), tywyll → yn dywyll ('dark'), tref → yn dref ('a town'). No word in c- or p- follows this yn in the chapter yet. A word beginning with a vowel or h- never changes: Mae Afon Wysg yn hir ('The river Wysg is long'), Mae'r ogof yn uchel ar y bryn ('The cave is high up on the hill'). After this yn, ll- and rh- stay unchanged too. Yn 'in' never causes soft mutation.

Dyma ('here is, here are') also causes soft mutation: Dyma Gymru ('Here is Wales'; c → g). In this book place names mutate like other words.

Some softened words have no yn or dyma before them: ynys fawr ('a big island', from mawr), y ddinas ('the city', from dinas), y goedwig ('the forest', from coedwig). These nouns are feminine (marked b. in the glosses). The Treigladau table, which gives the Pennod that explains each mutation, points to Pennod 2 for these; for now just read them.

Further location-table translations: Ble mae Caerllion? means “Where is Caerllion?”; Ble mae Llys Cynyr? means “Where is Cynyr’s court?”; Yng Nghwm Helyg, wrth yr afon means “In Cwm Helyg, by the river”. Ble mae Cymru? means “Where is Wales?”; Rhwng Iwerddon a Lloegr means “Between Ireland and England”. Mae Cymru’n fach means “Wales is small”.

The table’s gwlad fach means “a small country”.

Rhan 1 · Pennod 2

Teulu Cynyr

I. Wrth y tŷ mawr

Mae hi'n fore yng Nghwm Helyg. Mae'r teulu wrth y tŷ mawr yn Llys Cynyr. Dyma'r teulu: dyma deulu Cynyr.

yng Nghwm ← yn + Cwm · fore ← bore · bore

Dyma Cynyr. Mae Cynyr yn ddyn mawr, ac mae barf Cynyr yn fawr iawn. Barf fawr, barf hir, barf dda!

ddyn ← dyn · barf · dda ← da

Pwy yw'r wraig wrth Cynyr? Elen yw hi: Elen yw gwraig Cynyr. Elen yw mam Cai a Mali hefyd.

y wraig ← gwraig (b.) · teulu Cynyr

Pwy yw Cai? Cai yw mab Cynyr ac Elen. Mae Cai'n fachgen mawr, ond mae e'n ifanc.

mab + Cynyr = mab Cynyr · fachgen ← bachgen · ifanc: bachgen ↔ dyn

Pwy yw'r ferch? Mali yw'r ferch: Mali yw merch Cynyr ac Elen. Mae gwallt Mali'n hir ac yn dywyll. Cai yw brawd Mali, a Mali yw chwaer Cai.

y ferch ← merch (b.) · ferch ← merch (b.) · gwallt

A dyma Arth. Mae Arth yn fachgen bach. Mae Arth yn fach, ond mae gwallt Arth yn fawr iawn!

Mae plant yn y llys: Cai, Mali ac Arth. Cai yw'r plentyn mawr, ac Arth yw'r plentyn bach. Mae Arth yn y llys, ac mae e yn y teulu. Ond pwy yw tad Arth?

plentyn, plant

"Bore da, blant!" meddai Cynyr.

blant ← plant · meddai Cynyr → Cynyr: «…»

"Bore da, Cai. Bore da, Mali. Bore da, Arth," meddai Elen.

"Bore da, Mam," meddai Arth.

II. Y ci, y gath a'r ceffylau

Mae ci yn y llys hefyd: hen gi mawr. Pero yw enw'r ci. Mae Pero wrth y wal, ac mae e'n hen iawn.

hen gi ← ci · enw: Cai, Mali, Pero … · enw + y ci = enw'r ci

"Bore da, Mali! Nos da, Pero!" meddai Cai.

bore ↔ nos

"Nos da?" meddai Mali. "Mae hi'n fore, Cai!"

"Bore? Nos?" meddai Cynyr. "Mae Pero'n hen!"

Mae cath yn y llys hefyd. Mae'r gath yn fach ac yn ifanc. A'r enw? Cath yw enw'r gath!

y gath ← cath (b.) · gath ← cath

Ble mae'r ceffylau? Wrth y wal, wrth Pero. Mae ceffyl Cynyr yn hen geffyl mawr, ac mae ceffyl Cai'n ifanc. Mae Arth wrth yr hen geffyl mawr: ceffyl Cynyr.

ceffyl, ceffylau · hen geffyl ← ceffyl · geffyl ← ceffyl

"Ceffyl Cai yw'r ceffyl da!" meddai Cai.

"Ceffyl Cynyr yw'r ceffyl da!" meddai Arth.

Pwy yw'r fenyw fach wrth y tŷ mawr? Modlen yw hi: Modlen yw cogyddes y llys. Mae'r gogyddes yn fenyw fach, ac mae Pero wrth y gogyddes.

y fenyw ← menyw (b.) · cogyddes · y gogyddes ← cogyddes (b.) · yn fenyw ← menyw (b.) · wrth y gogyddes gogyddes ← cogyddes (b.)

III. Pwy yw e?

Mae'r plant wrth y wal.

"Pwy yw hi?" meddai Mali. "Mae hi'n fenyw fach, ac mae hi wrth y tŷ mawr."

"Modlen!" meddai Arth.

"Modlen yw hi." Pwy yw e? Mae e'n hen, ac mae e wrth y wal."

"Pero!"

"Pwy yw hi? Gwraig Cynyr yw hi, a mam Cai a Mali."

"Mam!" meddai Arth.

"Pwy yw e?" meddai Cai. "Mae e'n fawr, mae e'n ifanc, ac mae e'n dda iawn!"

dda ← da

"Ceffyl Cai!" meddai Arth.

"Ceffyl?" meddai Cai. "Cai yw e! Dyma'r dyn mawr!"

"Dyn?" meddai Mali. "Mam, mae Cai'n fachgen."

mae Cai'n fachgen Cai'n fachgen ↔ Cai yw mab Cynyr

"Mae Cai'n fab da," meddai Elen.

fab ← mab

"Cai yw'r brawd mawr, a dyma'r chwaer fach!" meddai Cai.

"Pwy yw e?" meddai Arth. "Mae e'n ddyn, ac mae e'n dad. Arth yw mab y dyn. Pwy yw e?"

dad ← tad · ddyn ← dyn

"Pwy yw e, Arth?"

"Tad Arth."

"Dad," meddai Mali, "pwy yw tad Arth?"

"…" meddai Cynyr.

"Arth yw brawd Cai, a Mali yw chwaer Arth," meddai Elen.

"Arth!" meddai Cynyr. "Dyma'r ceffyl mawr!"

"Ceffyl da!" meddai Arth.

Mae Arth wrth y ceffyl mawr, ac mae gwallt Arth yn fawr iawn. Ond ble mae tad Arth?

Nodyn (Saesneg)

Pwy yw …? means 'Who is …?'. To identify someone, that is, to say which person they are, Welsh uses X yw Y: Cai yw mab Cynyr ac Elen ('Cai is the son of Cynyr and Elen'). The two halves name the same person, and either can come first: Elen yw gwraig Cynyr ('Elen is Cynyr's wife'); Gwraig Cynyr yw hi, a mam Cai a Mali ('She is Cynyr's wife, and the mother of Cai and Mali'). Hi is 'she' and e is 'he': Pwy yw e? ('Who is he?'). For time, hi means 'it': Mae hi'n fore yng Nghwm Helyg ('It is morning in Cwm Helyg').

To describe someone, that is, to say what kind of person or thing they are, use the Pennod 1 pattern Mae X yn …, with soft mutation after yn: Mae Cai'n fachgen mawr, ond mae e'n ifanc ('Cai is a big boy, but he is young'). The first table sets the two patterns side by side. Look at the second half. If it is definite (one particular person or thing: a name, a noun with y/'r, or a phrase like mab Cynyr), use yw. If it is an adjective or an indefinite noun ('a …'), use Mae … yn; in this book so far an indefinite noun never comes before yw. So Modlen yw cogyddes y llys ('Modlen is the cook of the court'), but Mae'r gogyddes yn fenyw fach ('The cook is a small woman'). Mali's correction of Cai turns on this: Mam, mae Cai'n fachgen ('Mum, Cai is a boy').

There is no word here for 'of' or for English -'s: the owner simply follows the thing owned. Mab Cynyr is 'Cynyr's son' (literally 'son Cynyr'), ceffyl Cai is 'Cai's horse'. A 'the' belongs to the owner: enw'r ci ('the dog's name'), cogyddes y llys ('the cook of the court'). The first noun never takes y/'r of its own. The phrase is already definite, so it goes with yw: Pero yw enw'r ci ('Pero is the dog's name').

Every Welsh noun is either masculine or feminine. This is grammatical gender, marked g. and b. in the glosses, and it is learned with each word. For most words for people it follows sex (merch 'girl' and gwraig 'wife' are feminine, bachgen 'boy' is masculine), but cath 'cat' is feminine for any cat. After y/'r ('the'), a feminine singular noun takes soft mutation: y ferch ('the girl, the daughter'), y gath ('the cat'), y wraig ('the wife'), y fenyw ('the woman'), y gogyddes ('the cook') (from merch, cath, gwraig, menyw, cogyddes). Pwy yw'r ferch? ('Who is the girl?'). Masculine nouns and plurals do not change: y ci ('the dog'), y ceffyl ('the horse'), Mae'r plant wrth y wal ('The children are by the wall'). Ll- and rh- do not change after y either.

A feminine singular noun also softens the adjective after it: Barf fawr, barf hir, barf dda! ('A big beard, a long beard, a good beard!'; from mawr and da, while hir begins with h- and never changes). After a masculine noun the adjective stays as it is. Cai's boast has both: Cai yw'r brawd mawr, a dyma'r chwaer fach! ('Cai is the big brother, and here is the little sister!'). This explains the Pennod 1 words gwlad fach ('a small country') and y goedwig ('the forest').

Most adjectives come after the noun, but hen 'old' comes before it and softens it: hen gi ('an old dog'), and Mae ceffyl Cynyr yn hen geffyl mawr ('Cynyr's horse is a big old horse'). When hen is the predicate it follows yn like any adjective and stays hen: Mae Pero'n hen! ('Pero is old!').

The last two rows of the Treigladau table repeat Pennod 1: soft mutation after predicative yn (yn fachgen) and after dyma: Dyma'r teulu: dyma deulu Cynyr ('Here is the family: here is Cynyr's family'). Names of people never mutate in this book, so it is Dyma Cynyr ('Here is Cynyr'), though place names do (Dyma Gymru). Two softened words in the dialogue have a cause this book has not explained yet, so read them as set phrases for now: Bore da, blant! ('Good morning, children!', from plant) and Dad ('Dad', from tad), when Mali speaks to her father.

Table examples: Pwy yw Cai? — “Who is Cai?”; Mali yw merch Cynyr ac Elen — “Mali is Cynyr and Elen’s daughter”; Mae gwallt Mali’n hir — “Mali’s hair is long”; Pwy yw’r fenyw fach? — “Who is the small woman?”; Pwy yw tad Arth? — “Who is Arth’s father?”; Mae Arth yn fachgen bach — “Arth is a small boy”; barf Cynyr — “Cynyr’s beard”; Dyma Gymru — “Here is Wales”.

Nodyn (Saesneg)

This chapter sets two kinds of yn side by side. The new one comes before a verb-noun: the basic form of a Welsh verb, as listed in the vocabulary, such as rhedeg ('run, running'), bwyta ('eat, eating') or darllen ('read, reading'). Its ending never changes for who does the action. Mae … yn + verb-noun is the present tense and covers both English 'is doing' and 'does': Mae Arth yn rhedeg ('Arth is running'), Mae Pero'n cysgu wrth y drws ('Pero is sleeping by the door').

The other is predicative yn from Pennod 1, before an adjective (a describing word) or a noun. It links the subject to what is said about it, the predicate, and causes soft mutation: a regular change to the next word's first consonant. Here c becomes g, d becomes dd, b and m become f, and g drops: Mae gwallt Cai'n goch ('Cai's hair is red'), Mae hi'n fore ('It is morning'), Mae Cymru'n wlad fach ('Wales is a small country'). In Mae Pero'n hen gi du a gwyn ('Pero is an old black and white dog') the h of hen cannot change, and hen itself softens ci to gi. Yn + adjective can also say how an action happens: Mae hi'n cerdded yn araf ('She walks slowly'). Here yn araf describes the walking, and it follows the same mutation pattern.

The yn before a verb-noun causes no mutation: Mae Arth yn gweld y cleddyf ('Arth sees the sword'), Mae Mali'n darllen ('Mali is reading'). So it is yn gyflym but yn cario, yn ddu but yn darllen: after this yn, verbal nouns remain unchanged; adjectives take soft mutation where applicable. After a vowel both kinds are written 'n (Cai'n, Pero'n). Two actions or two descriptions can share one Mae by repeating yn after ac ('and', the form of a before a vowel): Mae e'n rhedeg ac yn bwyta! ('He is running and eating!'), Mae Arth yn fach ac yn gyflym ('Arth is small and quick').

o means 'from' and i means 'to, into'. After them y ('the') shrinks to 'r, as it does after any vowel: Mae Arth yn cario dŵr o'r afon ('Arth is carrying water from the river'); O'r stabl i'r neuadd! ('From the stable to the hall!'). When the article comes between, it is the article that matters, not o or i: in i'r goedwig ('into the forest'), coedwig becomes goedwig because it is a feminine singular noun after the article. The chapter also has i Cai: Mae Arth yn rhoi'r cleddyf pren i Cai ('Arth gives the wooden sword to Cai'); personal names never mutate in this book.

The Treigladau ('mutations') table collects the soft mutations so far, with the chapter where each began. Predicative yn softens: yn goch, yn ddu, yn gyflym. The new row is the exception: yn before a verb-noun changes nothing (yn gweld, yn bwyta, yn darllen). y ('the') softens a feminine singular noun; every Welsh noun is masculine or feminine, and the vocabulary marks feminine ones (b.). So cegin → y gegin ('the kitchen'), and gardd → yr ardd ('the garden': the g drops, and y becomes yr before a vowel). An adjective after a feminine singular noun softens too: y gath ddu ('the black cat'), y goedwig dywyll ('the dark forest', t → d). And dyma ('here is') softens the noun after it: Dyma ddrws y neuadd ('Here is the door of the hall').

Remaining reference translations: Mae Cai’n chwarae means “Cai is playing”; Mae’r cleddyf pren yn gyflym iawn means “The wooden sword is very fast”; Mae Cai’n codi cleddyf pren means “Cai is lifting a wooden sword”. In the verbal-noun table, yn gweld, yn gwneud and yn gweithio mean “seeing”, “making/doing” and “working”; yn bwyta, yn darllen and yn dod mean “eating”, “reading” and “coming”; yn codi, yn cario and yn cysgu mean “lifting/getting up”, “carrying” and “sleeping”. Mae Pero’n rhedeg o’r buarth, o’r llys, i’r goedwig means “Pero runs out of the farmyard, out of the court, into the forest”. Cath ddu means “a black cat”; dyma ddrws means “here is a door”.

Rhan 1 · Pennod 4

Ble mae Pero?

I. Ble mae Pero?

Mae hi'n nos yn Llys Cynyr, ac mae hi'n oer. Mae Modlen, y gogyddes, yn cau ffenest y gegin. Mae tân yn y neuadd, ac mae'r neuadd yn gynnes. Mae'r teulu yn y neuadd: Cynyr, Elen, Cai, Mali ac Arth. Mae Elen yn agor drws y neuadd, ac mae hi'n edrych ar y buarth. Ond ble mae Pero?

Nodyn (Saesneg)

This chapter teaches yes/no questions, their answers, and 'not'. Keep two kinds of sentence apart: ordinary Mae sentences, and identification sentences with yw (Pennod 2). Each has its own answer words.

Ydy …? In a Mae sentence with a definite subject, the question simply starts with Ydy instead of Mae; nothing else changes. A definite subject is a particular, known person or thing: a name (Pero), a pronoun such as e ('he, it'), or a noun with y, yr or 'r ('the'). Mae Pero yn y stabl ('Pero is in the stable') becomes Ydy Pero yn y stabl? ('Is Pero in the stable?'). So too Ydy'r goedwig yn bell? ('Is the forest far?') and, with a verb-noun, Ydy Pero'n cysgu yn y goedwig? ('Is Pero sleeping in the forest?').

There is no single word for 'yes' or 'no' here: you answer with the verb, Ydy ('yes, he/she/it is') or Nac ydy ('no, he/she/it isn't'). Ydy'r lamp yn gynnes? Ydy, mae'r lamp yn gynnes ('Is the lamp warm? Yes, the lamp is warm').

Dyw … ddim. For 'not', replace Mae with Dyw and put ddim after the subject: Dyw Pero ddim yn y stabl ('Pero isn't in the stable'); dyw Pero ddim yn dod ('Pero doesn't come'); Dyw'r sŵn ddim yn sŵn ci ('The noise isn't a dog's noise'). Positive and negative often stand together: Mae'r ceffylau yma, ond dyw Pero ddim yma ('The horses are here, but Pero isn't here'). Dyw … ddim is the southern form the book uses; treat it as a fixed frame for now. In this book so far every Ydy question and every Dyw sentence has a definite subject. Mae mwg ('There is smoke') has an indefinite one (some smoke, not 'the smoke'); questions and negatives about indefinite things work differently and are not used yet.

Ie and Nage. An identification sentence puts the important word first, then yw: Pero yw e ('It's Pero', literally 'Pero is it'). As a question it keeps the same words: Pero yw e? ('Is it Pero?'), Tân yw e? ('Is it fire?'). It does not start with a verb, so Ydy cannot answer it. Say Ie ('yes') or Nage ('no'): Cath yw e? Nage. ('Is it a cat? No.'); Ie, Pero yw e! ('Yes, it's Pero!'). A quick test: a question starting with Ydy takes Ydy or Nac ydy; one starting with a noun before yw takes Ie or Nage.

The Treigladau ('mutations') table adds new words to known rules. Predicative yn, which links a subject to a description, causes soft mutation, a regular change to the first consonant: tawel → yn dawel ('quiet'), cynnes → yn gynnes ('warm'), pell → yn bell ('far'), gwyrdd → yn wyrdd ('green'); so t → d, c → g, p → b, and g drops. But ll and rh do not change after this yn: Mae'r mwg yn llwyd ('The smoke is grey'). y ('the') softens a feminine singular noun: y goeden ('the tree'), y garreg ('the stone'); plurals do not change: y coed ('the trees'). An adjective after a feminine singular noun softens too: in mae Elen yn fenyw dawel ('Elen is a quiet woman') yn softens menyw and the feminine noun softens tawel. After masculine drws nothing changes: drws gwyrdd ('a green door'). Last, ar dân ('on fire'), ar gau ('closed') and ar agor ('open') are fixed phrases for now: ar ('on') softens tân and cau, and agor, starting with a vowel, cannot change. The table points to Pennod 16 for this rule.

Remaining example translations: Ydy’r goedwig ar dân? means “Is the forest on fire?”; Dyw’r goedwig ddim yn bell means “The forest is not far away”; Dyw’r coed ddim ar dân means “The trees are not on fire”; Mae’r mwg yn llwyd means “The smoke is grey”.

Nodyn (Saesneg)

This chapter gives the present tense of bod ('to be') for 'I' and 'you', beside the 'he' and 'she' forms you already know. In these statements the verb comes first and the person after it: dw i ('I am'), rwyt ti ('you are'), mae e ('he is'), mae hi ('she is'). Ti is the familiar 'you'. Myrddin uses it to the children, and Mali uses it to Arth and to Dafi.

After the verb comes yn, shortened to 'n after a vowel, and then a verb-noun, an adjective or a noun. A verb-noun is the dictionary form of a verb, such as darllen ('to read') or dysgu ('to learn, to teach'). It never changes for the person, because bod shows who is doing it: Dw i'n dysgu, ac rwyt ti'n dysgu ('I am teaching, and you are learning'). The same form covers 'I read' and 'I am reading'. Before an adjective or a noun, yn normally causes soft mutation (words beginning with ll and rh stay unchanged, as in Pennod 1), which is a change to certain first consonants of the next word: Dw i'n ddewr! ('I'm brave!', from dewr), Rwyt ti'n wyn! ('You're white!', that is, pale, from gwyn), Mae e'n goch ('He is red', from coch). A verb-noun after yn does not change: Dw i'n darllen ('I read').

Questions. To ask a yes/no question, Welsh uses the question form of the verb; there is no extra word like English 'do'. Rwyt ti becomes Wyt ti: Wyt ti'n ddewr, Arth? ('Are you brave, Arth?'). For 'he', 'she' or a name, the question form is Ydy: Ydy e'n ddraig? ('Is he a dragon?'), Ydy Myrddin yn ddewin, Dafi? ('Is Myrddin a wizard, Dafi?'). Pwy ('who') and sut ('how') also use wyt ti: Pwy wyt ti? ('Who are you?'), Sut wyt ti? ('How are you?').

Answers. These questions have no single word for 'yes' or 'no'. You answer with the verb itself, in the person that fits the answer, so a question about 'you' gets an answer about 'I': Wyt ti'n darllen? ('Do you read?') → Ydw ('Yes, I do') or Nac ydw ('No, I don't'). For 'he', 'she' or a name: Ydy e'n ddraig? → Ydy ('Yes, he is') or Nac ydy ('No, he isn't'). A question that starts with a noun instead of the verb, such as Hud yw e? ('Is it magic?'), is answered Ie ('Yes') or Nage ('No'), as in Pennod 4: Nage. Sbectol yw hi ('No. They're spectacles', literally 'it is spectacles').

Negatives. To say 'not', use the negative form of the verb and ddim ('not'), then yn: Dw i ddim yn darllen ('I don't read'), Dwyt ti ddim yn hapus ('You aren't happy'), Dyw Dafi ddim yn drist ('Dafi isn't sad'). Dw i stays the same, rwyt ti becomes dwyt ti, and mae becomes dyw. After ddim, yn is written in full, and it still causes soft mutation: drist, from trist ('sad').

Saying who you are. To say who or what you are, put the noun first and dw i after it: Arth dw i ('I'm Arth'), Mali dw i, merch Cynyr ('I'm Mali, Cynyr's daughter'), Dewin dw i ('I'm a wizard'), Athro Arth dw i ('I'm Arth's teacher'). This is the same order as Dafi yw e ('He's Dafi'), with dw i in place of yw. The noun at the front does not mutate. A ti? means 'And you?': Myrddin asks it, then Pwy wyt ti? ('Who are you?'), and Mali answers Mali dw i.

Eisiau ('want'). Eisiau follows the verb directly, with no yn: Mae e eisiau bwyd ('He wants food'), Dw i eisiau mynd i'r llys ('I want to go to the llys'). Compare Dw i'n hapus ('I am happy') with Dw i eisiau mynd i'r llys ('I want to go to the llys'): eisiau follows dw i directly. Mae e'n goch ('He is red') has yn; Mae e eisiau bwyd ('He wants food') does not.

Nodyn (Saesneg)

This chapter shows two ways of asking and denying 'is …?', and which one you use depends on the subject, the thing the sentence is about. In these examples bara ('bread'), caws ('cheese'), draig ('a dragon') and rhywbeth ('something') are indefinite: they do not point to one particular thing. Definite subjects include nouns with 'the', names, pronouns such as e and hi, and phrases such as plât Cai ('Cai's plate'), even without y. Welsh has no word for 'a', so draig alone means 'a dragon'. A subject is definite when it is a particular, known thing: a noun with y or 'r, such as y bara ('the bread'); a name, such as Pero or Dafi; e ('he, it') or hi ('she, it'); or a noun followed by its owner, such as plât Cai ('Cai's plate'), which is definite even without y.

In a statement both kinds use mae: Mae bara ar y plât ('There is bread on the plate') and Mae'r bara ar y plât ('The bread is on the plate'). English adds 'there is' for the indefinite one; Welsh does not.

Questions are different. With an indefinite subject, the question begins with Oes ('is there?'), a form of bod ('to be'): Oes bara yn y gegin? ('Is there bread in the kitchen?'). The answer is Oes ('Yes, there is') or Nac oes ('No, there isn't'): "Oes," meddai Modlen ('"Yes," said Modlen'). Recall from Pennod 5 «Does dim bara …»–040: Ydy e’n ddraig? ('Is he a dragon?') → Ydy ('Yes, he is'). With a definite subject, use Ydy …?, answered Ydy or Nac ydy.

Negatives split the same way. With an indefinite subject, say Does dim … ('there is no …'): Does dim bara ar y plât! ('There's no bread on the plate!'), Does dim tân dan y bwrdd ('There's no fire under the table'). With a definite subject, say Dyw … ddim ('… is not'), as in this chapter: Dyw'r mwg ddim yn dod o'r tân! ('The smoke isn't coming from the fire!'). So y bara takes Ydy and Dyw … ddim, never Oes or Does dim.

Rhywbeth ('something') is indefinite, so it takes Oes: Arth, oes rhywbeth dan y bwrdd? ('Arth, is there something under the table?'). Its opposite is dim byd ('nothing'), which takes the place of dim: Does dim byd dan y bwrdd ('There's nothing under the table').

The pronouns e and hi behave like definite nouns: Dyw e ddim yn gi drwg ('He isn't a bad dog'). The other persons keep their own forms from Pennod 5: Wyt ti'n bwyta'r bara? ('Are you eating the bread?') → Nac ydw! ('No, I'm not!').

Treigladau (mutations). Every Welsh noun is either masculine or feminine; the glosses mark feminine nouns (b.), short for benywaidd ('feminine'). After y or 'r ('the'), a feminine singular noun takes soft mutation, as in Pennod 2 (except words beginning with ll and rh): cadair ('chair') → y gadair ('the chair'), mainc ('bench') → y fainc ('the bench'). The story also has y gynffon ('the tail', from cynffon). Masculine nouns do not change after y: y bwrdd ('the table'), y plât ('the plate'). An adjective after a feminine singular noun normally softens too: ar y gadair fawr ('on the big chair', from mawr). One exception to the soft mutation after yn before an adjective: words beginning with ll do not change, so Dyw Dafi ddim yn llawn ('Dafi isn't full').

After a ('and'), c changes to ch: bara a chaws ('bread and cheese'), a chynffon fach goch hefyd ('and a little red tail too'). This is a different change, called the aspirate mutation. In this book so far it is shown only with c. The dialogue uses the conversational short question A ti? ('And you?').

Full reference translations: Oes rhywbeth yn yr het? — ‘Is there anything in the hat?’; Nac oes. Does dim byd yn yr het — ‘No. There is nothing in the hat’. Y gadair and y fainc mean ‘the chair’ and ‘the bench’; bara a chaws and a chynffon mean ‘bread and cheese’ and ‘and a tail’. The first table gives a direct English translation of each story example.

Nodyn (Saesneg)

This chapter teaches the command form, which grammar books call the imperative: the form you use to tell someone to do something. Most commands here address one familiar person, using the ti form (for a friend, a child, a family member, an animal). A command needs no word for 'you'. A name, if there is one, is simply added: Gwranda, Arth! ('Listen, Arth!').

The starting point is the verb-noun (berfenw): the dictionary form of a verb, the form you already use after yn, as in Mae Arth yn gwrando ('Arth is listening'). Some commands are just the verb-noun said as an order: Edrych! ('Look!'), Aros, a gwranda eto ('Wait, and listen again'), Arth, dal y bwced ('Arth, hold the bucket'). Others have their own short form, which you learn together with the verb-noun: gwrando → Gwranda! ('Listen!'), sefyll → Saf ar un goes! ('Stand on one leg!'), cymryd → Cymer bastai! ('Have a pie!', literally 'Take a pie!'), rhoi → Rho wellt i'r ceffylau! ('Give straw to the horses!'). Two common southern ones look nothing like their verb-nouns: dod ('to come') → Dere yma ('Come here'), and mynd ('to go') → Cer i'r afon! ('Go to the river!'). Cer mas! means 'Get out!' (mas is 'out'). No single rule tells you which form a verb takes, so in this book so far, learn each command as you meet it. When Modlen calls all the children, she says Blant, dewch yma! ('Children, come here!'). Dewch is the form for more than one person. It is here for recognition; the commands to learn now are the ti forms.

To say 'don't', use Paid â + verb-noun: Paid â siarad! ('Don't talk!'), Paid â darllen! ('Don't read!'). Before a vowel, â becomes ag: Paid ag edrych ('Don't look'). Paid can also stand alone: Dafi, paid! ('Dafi, don't!'). Compare Dw i ddim yn edrych ('I'm not looking') with Paid ag edrych.

â is also a preposition meaning 'with': Mae Cai'n chwarae â'r cleddyf pren ('Cai is playing with the wooden sword'). Some verbs always take it. Cyffwrdd â means 'to touch': Paid â chyffwrdd â'r pasteiod! ('Don't touch the pies!'). With dod and mynd, â means bringing or taking: dere â dŵr ('bring water', literally 'come with water'), Cer â'r bara i'r neuadd! ('Take the bread to the hall!').

A mutation is a regular change to the first sound of a word, caused by the word before it. After â, a word beginning with c takes the aspirate mutation: c becomes ch, as in cyffwrdd → â chyffwrdd. So cyffwrdd becomes â chyffwrdd. A word that already begins with ch, such as chwarae, stays as it is: Cai, paid â chwarae! ('Cai, don't play!').

The soft mutation is a different change: g drops, p becomes b, c becomes g, and so on. The direct object of a command is the thing the order is about, straight after the command, and it takes the soft mutation: Rho wellt! from gwellt, Cymer bastai! from pastai. When the object begins with 'the' (y or 'r), the command does not change it: Rho'r bwced yma ('Give the bucket here'), Dal y ci! ('Catch the dog!'). 'The' still has its own rule from Pennod 2: it softens a feminine singular noun. The story and grammar table give mae e'n bwyta'r bastai ('he eats the pie'). The input column headed berfenw gives verb-nouns, not affirmative commands: siarad ('to talk') and darllen ('to read') follow paid â to form negative commands.

Here un goes ('one leg', from coes) and un bastai ('one pie', from pastai) are recognition phrases. The general un + feminine noun mutation pattern is taught in Pennod 14; this chapter does not require producing it.

Nodyn (Saesneg)

For possession, saying that someone has something, the southern pattern used here says the thing is with them, using gyda ('with'): Mae cleddyf gyda Cai ('Cai has a sword', literally 'a sword is with Cai'). In this pattern the order is Mae, then the thing, then gyda, then the owner. Other words can follow: Mae pasteiod gyda hi ar y plât mawr ('She has pies on the big plate').

After gyda, use the pronouns fi, ti, fe and hi: Mae clogyn newydd gyda fi! ('I have a new cloak!'), Mae ffrind gyda ti ('You have a friend'), Mae tarian gyda fe ('He has a shield'), Mae pasteiod gyda hi ('She has pies'). A name stays as it is, because personal names never mutate (never change their first sound). Before a vowel sound, gyda becomes gydag: Mae cleddyf gyda Cai, ond mae draig gydag Arth ('Cai has a sword, but Arth has a dragon').

The thing owned is almost always indefinite here. It has no 'the': 'a sword', 'a present', 'money'. So these sentences work like the 'there is' sentences of Pennod 6. A question begins Oes …?, the answers are Oes ('Yes') and Nac oes ('No'), and the negative is Does dim …. Cai asks, Mali, oes anrheg gyda ti? ('Mali, have you got a present?'), and Mali says Oes. Arth answers Nac oes. Does dim anrheg gyda fi ('No. I haven't got a present'). Likewise Does dim arian gyda fi ('I have no money'). Myrddin turns Arth's words into a question just with his voice: Does dim byd gyda ti? ('You have nothing?').

Keep three ideas apart. Cleddyf Cai yw e ('It's Cai's sword') says whose sword it is: as in Pennod 2, the owner simply follows the thing, with no word for 'of'. Mae cleddyf gyda Cai ('Cai has a sword') says what Cai has. Mae Cai'n cael cleddyf go iawn ('Cai gets a real sword') says what he receives: cael ('to get') is the other side of rhoi ('to give').

A verb-noun is the dictionary form of a verb, the form used after yn. Three verb-nouns here take a second verb-noun straight after them, with no word for 'to': gallu ('to be able, can'), hoffi ('to like') and cael, which before a verb-noun means 'to be allowed to'. Mae Cai'n gallu marchogaeth ('Cai can ride'), Dw i ddim yn gallu darllen ('I can't read'), Dw i'n gallu dysgu Cai! ('I can teach Cai!'), Dw i'n hoffi marchogaeth! ('I like riding!'), Dw i'n cael dal y cleddyf? ('Am I allowed to hold the sword?'). The second verb-noun does not mutate. Hoffi can also take a noun: Dw i'n hoffi'r anrheg ('I like the present'). Questions are made as in Pennod 5: Wyt ti'n gallu codi'r cleddyf? ('Can you lift the sword?') Nac ydw! ('No!').

The mutation table adds a group of prepositions. After ar ('on'), wrth ('by'), i ('to, for'), o ('from, of') and dan ('under'), the next word takes the soft mutation, a softening of its first sound: m becomes f, d becomes dd, c becomes g. Examples: Clogyn newydd i farchog newydd ('A new cloak for a new knight', from marchog), wrth ddrws y neuadd ('by the door of the hall', from drws), ar gadair ('on a chair', from cadair), ar garreg ('on a stone', from carreg). When 'the' comes between, the preposition does not change the noun: ar y bwrdd hir ('on the long table'). Only the Pennod 2 rule for 'the' with a feminine noun applies: ar y darian ('on the shield', from tarian). Names do not change: mae hi'n rhoi'r clogyn i Cai ('she gives the cloak to Cai'). The book returns to these prepositions in Pennod 16.

Two fixed phrases are worth learning whole for now. Mae'n ddrwg gyda fi means 'I'm sorry' (literally 'it is bad with me'). Ages use oed ('years old') after the number: Mae Cai'n bymtheg oed ('Cai is fifteen'), where pymtheg softens after yn like any description. In Dim ond un ar ddeg oed wyt ti! ('You're only eleven!'), the age comes before wyt ti; for now, treat this as a fixed age pattern.

The bare-noun preposition examples in this chapter are recognition material: the general mutation pattern after prepositions is taught in Pennod 16. The open shield model here uses the already familiar ar y darian (“on the shield”).

Reference translations: Does dim ceffyl gyda fe — “He hasn’t got a horse”; Oes cleddyf gyda Cai? Oes — “Does Cai have a sword? Yes”; Rwyt ti’n cael dal y cleddyf — “You are allowed to hold the sword”.

Nodyn (Saesneg)

This chapter completes the present tense of bod ('to be') with the plural persons. Person means who a sentence is about (the speaker, the one spoken to, or someone else); plural means more than one. Beside the singular forms dw i ('I am'), rwyt ti ('you are') and mae e / mae hi ('he / she is'), stand dyn ni ('we are'), dych chi ('you are', to more than one person, or politely to one) and maen nhw ('they are'). As before, yn (shortened to 'n after a vowel) links them to a verb-noun, the dictionary form of a verb: Dyn ni'n mynd i'r afon heddiw ('We're going to the river today'), Maen nhw'n byw yno ('They live there'). Before a description, yn softens the next word as usual (except ll and rh): dyn ni'n wlyb ('we're wet', from gwlyb).

Nhw ('they') can mean people (Arth and Mali in the boat) or things (the fish in Maen nhw'n byw yno). Maen goes only with nhw. When the subject is a noun, even a plural noun or two names, the verb stays mae: Mae'r plant yn eistedd wrth Myrddin ('The children sit by Myrddin'). Pawb ('everyone') also takes mae: Mae pawb yn wlyb ('Everyone is wet').

The negative ('not') follows dw i ddim and dyw e ddim: dyn ni ddim ('we are not'), dych chi ddim ('you are not'), and for 'they' dyn nhw ddim, not maen nhw ddim, just as mae e becomes dyw e ddim. Yn still comes before a verb-noun: Dyn ni ddim yn gweld pysgod ('We don't see any fish'), Dych chi ddim yn nofio ('You don't swim'), Dyn nhw ddim yn gwybod ('They don't know'). A place word such as yma ('here') needs no linking yn, as after mae: Dyn nhw ddim yma! ('They aren't here!').

In the southern speech of this book, a question with ni or chi is the statement said as a question: Dych chi'n byw yn y tŵr? ('Do you live in the tower?'), Dyn ni'n pysgota yn y cwch? ('Are we fishing in the boat?'). A question word goes in front: Sut dych chi'n sych? ('How are you dry?'). For a yes/no question about 'them' the story uses Ydyn nhw …?: Ydyn nhw'n fawr? ('Are they big?').

As in Penodau 4 and 5, the answer repeats the verb in the right person: Ydyn and Nac ydyn ('yes', 'no') for 'we' or 'they', Ydych and Nac ydych for 'you'. Choose by who the answer is about. Arth, in the boat, asks Dyn ni'n pysgota yn y cwch?, and Myrddin, on the bank, answers Ydych ('Yes, you are'). Asked Ydyn nhw'n fawr?, he says Ydyn ('Yes, they are'). To Dych chi eisiau gweld y byd dan y dŵr? ('Do you want to see the world under the water?'), Arth answers Ydyn! ('Yes, we do!') and Mali Nac ydyn! ('No, we don't!'). Asked of one person, dych chi gets a singular answer: Dych chi'n hen iawn? ('Are you very old?') Ydw ('Yes, I am').

Chi is also the polite 'you' to one person. Arth asks Myrddin wyt ti'n byw yn y tŵr? ('do you live in the tower?'), and Mali corrects him: Mae Myrddin yn hen, ac mae e'n athro. Dim ti: chi! ('Myrddin is old, and he's a teacher. Not ti: chi!'). The children say chi to Myrddin but ti to Dafi and Pero: Wyt ti'n hoffi'r afon, Dafi? ('Do you like the river, Dafi?') beside A chi, Myrddin? Dych chi'n hoffi'r afon? ('And you, Myrddin? Do you like the river?').

A command (the form that tells someone to do something) has a ti form and a chi form. Pennod 7 gave the ti forms; the chi forms, for more than one person or one person politely, are Dewch! ('Come!'), Ewch! ('Go!'), Edrychwch! ('Look!') and Arhoswch! ('Wait!'). Edrychwch adds -wch to edrych; arhoswch adds -wch to arhos-, with an h that aros lacks. Dere and dewch, cer and ewch are not built this way: learn them as pairs. This book uses only these four chi commands for now. Myrddin tells the children Arhoswch. Edrychwch ar y dŵr ('Wait. Look at the water'). But Mali, to Arth alone, says Edrych, Arth! ('Look, Arth!').

Reference translations: Dafi, wyt ti’n gallu hedfan? — “Dafi, can you fly?”; Dych chi’n sych — “You’re dry”; Dyn ni’n pysgota — “We’re fishing”.

Pysgodyn!

Nodyn (Saesneg)

A possessive is a word that says whose something is: 'my', 'your', 'his', 'her'. In Welsh it comes before the noun, and a short pronoun, the echo pronoun, follows the noun: fy nwylo i ('my hands'), dy draed di ('your feet'), ei geg e ('his mouth'), ei cheg hi ('her mouth'). The echo pronouns are i, di, e and hi; di is the form ti takes after dy. The story always adds the echo, but it can be left out: Pensum A accepts fy nhraed as well as fy nhraed i ('my feet').

A possessive can change the first sound of the next word, depending on the possessive and on that sound. Such a change is called a mutation; this chapter shows three kinds.

Fy ('my') takes the nasal mutation. In the story p becomes mh, t becomes nh, d becomes n and g becomes ng: fy mhysgod i ('my fish', from pysgod), fy nhraed i ('my feet', from traed), fy nwylo i ('my hands', from dwylo), fy nannedd i ('my teeth', from dannedd), fy ngwallt i ('my hair', from gwallt). Ll and a vowel do not change: Fy llyn i yw e! ('It's my lake!'), Fy afon i yw hi! ('It's my river!').

Dy ('your', to one person you call ti) and ei meaning 'his' take the soft mutation, the change you know from yn and from y before a feminine singular noun: dy draed di ('your feet'), dy gefn di ('your back', from cefn), dy ddannedd di ('your teeth'), ei ben e ('his head', from pen), ei gorff e ('his body', from corff), ei gynffon e ('his tail'). A g simply disappears: dy wallt di ('your hair', from gwallt). Unlike yn and y, dy and ei 'his' also soften ll: ei law e ('his hand', from llaw), dy lygaid di ('your eyes', from llygaid). A vowel does not change: ei esgyll e ('his fins').

Ei meaning 'her' takes the aspirate mutation. In the story c becomes ch and p becomes ph: ei phen hi ('her head'), ei chorff hi ('her body'), ei chynffon hi ('her tail'). Because ei 'his' and ei 'her' look and sound the same, the mutation and the echo pronoun tell you which is meant: ei gynffon e ('his tail'), but ei chynffon hi ('her tail').

Ein ('our'), eich ('your', to more than one person, or politely to one) and eu ('their') work the same way, with ni, chi and nhw as echo pronouns. Here they are for recognition only. In the consonant-initial examples here, the consonants after ein, eich and eu remain unchanged. Before a vowel, ein and eu add h-; eich does not. Those vowel patterns are for later study: Dyma ein llyn ni ('Here is our lake'), Beth yw eich enwau chi? ('What are your names?'), Mae eu llygaid nhw'n fawr ('Their eyes are big').

Keep three patterns apart. Mae cynffon gyda fe ('He has a tail', the pattern of Pennod 8) says what someone has. Mae ei gynffon e'n gyflym ('His tail is fast') talks about a thing known to be his. With a name there is no possessive word: as in Pennod 2, the owner simply follows the thing, as in llaw Myrddin ('Myrddin's hand'). The first two meet when Arth asks Ble mae fy nwylo i? ('Where are my hands?') and Mali answers Does dim dwylo gyda ti! ('You haven't got hands!').

A possessive phrase can fill the X of the X yw Y pattern (Pennod 2): Fy afon i yw hi! ('It's my river!'). The pronoun at the end follows the gender of the thing meant. Mali's Dy wallt di yw hi! ('It's your hair!') points to Arth's fin, asgell, a feminine noun; Arth's Dy wallt di yw e! points to Mali's back, cefn, a masculine noun.

Body words with irregular plurals: llaw, dwylo ('hand, hands'), troed, traed ('foot, feet'), dant, dannedd ('tooth, teeth'), asgell, esgyll ('fin, fins'). The first table sets out phrases from the story for each possessive. The last table gathers the mutation triggers of Rhan 1; its rows marked Pennod 14 and 16 preview triggers that those chapters teach fully.

Further table translations: cynffon Mali means “Mali’s tail”. In the cumulative mutation table, yn fawr means “big”, yn ddraig “a dragon”, yn bysgod “fish”, and yn llawn “full”; yn rhedeg means “running”. Dyma fara means “Here is bread”; dyma wers “Here is a lesson”. Y ferch, y gegin, y bont and y llaw mean “the girl”, “the kitchen”, “the bridge” and “the hand”. Merch fach, het ddu and deilen fach mean “a small girl”, “a black hat” and “a small leaf”. Hen gi, hen gwch and hen bont mean “an old dog”, “an old boat” and “an old bridge”. Rho wellt! and Rho’r bwced! mean “Give straw!” and “Give the bucket!”; the article in the second phrase prevents mutation of bwced. Bara a chaws means “bread and cheese”; â chyffwrdd is the â + touching fragment from Paid â chyffwrdd (“Don’t touch”). Ar gau, wrth ddrws and i farchog mean “closed”, “by a door” and “to a knight”. Un goes, un bastai and un llaw mean “one leg”, “one pie” and “one hand”.

Nodyn (Saesneg)

This chapter's new pattern is the perfect: the verb form that looks back from the present at something that has happened. In this chapter it usually presents a completed event whose result is still in view. Welsh builds it by putting wedi in the place of yn. Mae Dafi'n bwyta'r pasteiod means 'Dafi is eating the pies'; Mae Dafi wedi bwyta'r pasteiod! means 'Dafi has eaten the pies!'. So Mae'r jwg wedi torri ('The jug has broken'; English often says 'is broken').

A verb-noun is the dictionary form of a verb, such as bwyta ('to eat'): the form that follows yn in Mae Dafi'n bwyta. The same verb-noun follows wedi, and it never mutates (never changes its first sound): wedi bwyta, wedi torri ('has eaten, has broken'). The linking yn before a verb-noun commonly contracts to 'n after a vowel (locative yn remains distinct, as in Dyn ni yn yr afon, ‘We are in the river’), but wedi simply replaces the linking yn, with no 'n left over: Mae Dafi wedi bwyta ('Dafi has eaten'), never Mae Dafi'n wedi.

Everything before wedi stays as in the yn sentences of Penodau 3, 5 and 9; only yn changes. Dw i wedi bod yn bysgodyn! ('I've been a fish!'), Rwyt ti wedi blino ('You're tired'), Dyn ni wedi bod yn yr afon gyda Pero! ('We've been in the river with Pero!'), Maen nhw wedi mynd, Cai! ('They've gone, Cai!'). Bod is the verb-noun 'to be', so wedi bod means 'has been, have been'. The story has no chi form with wedi yet. The first table sets the two patterns side by side: Dyn ni'n glanhau'r gegin nawr ('We're cleaning the kitchen now'), and when the work is done, Mae'r plant wedi glanhau'r gegin ('The children have cleaned the kitchen').

Questions and negatives also work as before, because the verb at the front is still a form of bod. Myrddin asks Wyt ti wedi dysgu rhywbeth, Arth? ('Have you learnt something?'), and Arth answers Ydw ('Yes'). Modlen asks Wyt ti wedi bwyta'r pasteiod? ('Have you eaten the pies?') and Cai answers Nac ydw! ('No!'). In the negative, ddim comes before wedi: Dw i ddim wedi bwyta'r pasteiod ('I haven't eaten the pies').

Two questions are learnt whole for now: Beth sy wedi digwydd? ('What has happened?') and Pwy sy wedi bwyta'r pasteiod? ('Who has eaten the pies?'). In these questions, beth or pwy asks which thing or person did it, and sy is the form of bod used in that pattern; treat them as fixed phrases. The answers use the ordinary pattern: Mae rhywbeth wedi digwydd ('Something has happened').

Choosing between yn and wedi is a matter of meaning, not of a time word. In this chapter yn shows an action in progress, and wedi looks back at one that has been completed (elsewhere the yn pattern can also describe states and habits). Nawr ('now') appears with both: Dw i'n bwyta nawr! ('I'm eating now!') and nawr mae'r pasteiod wedi mynd ('now the pies have gone'). When Dafi says Dafi'n bwyta pasteiod ('Dafi eating pies'), the pies are already gone, so Mali corrects him: rwyt ti wedi bwyta'r pasteiod ('you have eaten the pies').

Wedi blino means 'tired' (literally 'having tired'), and wedi takes the place of yn here too: mae'r plant yn wlyb ac wedi blino ('the children are wet and tired'). Yn barod is a fixed phrase meaning 'ready' (Ydy'r cawl yn barod? 'Is the cawl ready?') or 'already' (Mae'r ffwrn yn boeth yn barod! 'The oven is hot already!'). In Dw i ddim wedi gwneud y cawl eto ('I haven't made the cawl yet'), eto means 'yet'; its other uses in this chapter, such as mae hi'n codi'r llwy eto ('she raises the spoon again'), mean 'again'.

The last table gathers mutations met in earlier chapters. After fy ('my') comes the nasal mutation (c becomes ngh, p becomes mh): fy nghegin i ('my kitchen'), fy mhasteiod i ('my pies'). After dy ('your') and ei ('his') comes the soft mutation, a softening of the first sound (t becomes d, p becomes b, c becomes g): dy drwyn di ('your nose', from trwyn), ei ben e ('his head', from pen), ei gynffon e ('his tail', from cynffon). After yn, an adjective softens too, except one beginning with ll or rh: yn ddig ('angry', from dig), yn boeth ('hot', from poeth).

Reference translations: Wyt ti wedi bwyta, Cai? — “Have you eaten, Cai?”; Mae’r cawl wedi llosgi — “The soup has burnt”; wedi llosgi — “has/have burnt”.

II. Ddoe

"Ddoe. Yn gyntaf, es i i'r afon gyda Myrddin, Arth a Pero. Wnes i eistedd yn yr hen gwch gydag Arth, a wnes i bysgota, ond dw i ddim yn hoffi pysgota. Wnes i weld Dafi'n pysgota gyda mwg, a wnes i weld Pero'n nofio. Wedyn, meddai Myrddin: Dych chi eisiau gweld y byd dan y dŵr? Wnes i nofio dan y dŵr: pysgodyn bach, gyda chen ar fy nghorff i ac asgell ar fy nghefn i! Wnes i weld y pysgod bach yn cuddio eu pennau nhw. Ac meddai'r pysgod: Mae ein brenin ni yn y llyn! Gwelais i benhwyad mawr yn y llyn dwfn, a wnes i ofni ei ddannedd e. Wedyn, wnes i guddio dan y bont gydag Arth. Yn sydyn, wnes i weld llaw fawr Myrddin yn y dŵr. Wnes i weld Cai'n cysgu ar y lan yn yr haul: y marchog dewr! Yn olaf, des i i'r llys gyda Myrddin, Arth a Pero, yn wlyb ac wedi blino. Ond mae Myrddin yn sych, wrth gwrs. Diwrnod gwych!"

"Dw i ddim wedi anghofio," meddai Mali. "Mae'r bont yn y dyddiadur!"

Nawr mae Mali'n chwerthin.

"Wyt ti'n cofio'r gegin hefyd?" meddai Arth.

"Wrth gwrs. Dw i ddim yn anghofio dim byd," meddai Mali. "Gwranda, Arth."

Mae hi'n darllen eto, yn dawel ac yn araf.

III. Neithiwr

"Neithiwr. Noson ofnadwy yn y gegin! Yn gyntaf, gwelais i'r llanast: dim pasteiod, blawd ar y bwrdd a llaeth ar y fainc. Jwg wedi torri, cawl du yn y crochan, a chyllell yn y cawl! Wedyn, wnes i ffeindio olion traed bach yn y blawd, a wnes i achub Pero. Meddai Modlen: Draig yn fy nghegin i! Yn olaf, wnes i chwerthin: Modlen yn wyn, a Cai yn wyn hefyd! Ac nawr mae gwaith gyda Dafi."

neithiwr = ddoe, yn y nos · gwelais i = wnes i weld · a chyllell ← cyllell

"Ac mae Dafi'n hapus iawn yn y gegin nawr!" meddai Arth. "A neithiwr ces i gawl!"

cael → ces i · ces i gawl ← cawl

Mae Mali'n rhoi'r dyddiadur i Arth, ac mae e'n edrych ar y llyfr.

"Dw i ddim yn gallu darllen y dyddiadur," meddai Arth, "ond dw i'n gallu cofio'r cawl!"

"A heddiw, Mali?" meddai Arth. "Wyt ti wedi ysgrifennu heddiw?"

"Ydw," meddai Mali. "Dw i wedi ysgrifennu heddiw yn barod."

Ond nawr dyw Mali ddim yn chwerthin.

"Beth wnest ti heddiw?" meddai Arth.

IV. Y dyn ar y ffordd

"Heddiw. Es i ar y ffordd wrth y llys gyda Pero. Clywais i sŵn ceffyl. Wedyn, gwelais i ddyn rhyfedd ar y ffordd. Ceffyl mawr du. Clogyn tywyll, a draig fach goch ar y clogyn. Dieithryn yw e: dyn newydd yn y cwm. Meddai'r dieithryn: Ferch, oes bachgen un ar ddeg oed yn y cwm? Cwestiwn rhyfedd! Wnes i ateb: Mae bachgen pymtheg oed yn y llys. Mae e'n fawr, ac mae e eisiau bwyd. Yn olaf, es i i'r llys yn gyflym, gyda Pero. Wnes i deimlo'n oer, yn oer iawn. Nawr mae Pero'n cysgu wrth y tân, ond dw i ddim yn cysgu. Diwrnod rhyfedd."

ffordd: llys → tref · clywed → clywais i · ddyn ← dyn · rhyfedd: ceffyl yn darllen! · deimlo ← teimlo: «Dw i’n oer!»

Mae Arth yn chwerthin.

"Mae bachgen pymtheg oed yn y llys: Cai! Ateb gwych, Mali!" "Ond wnest ti ateb y cwestiwn?"

"Wnes i ateb y dieithryn," meddai Mali. "Ateb yw e, ond dyw e ddim yn ateb da."

Yn sydyn, dyw Arth ddim yn chwerthin.

"Mali…" meddai e. "Dw i'n un ar ddeg oed."

"Dw i'n gwybod, Arth," meddai Mali. "Cwestiwn ofnadwy yw e."

Mae hi'n noson dywyll, ac mae'r gegin yn dawel iawn.

"Pwy yw'r dieithryn?" meddai Arth. "Beth mae e eisiau?" "Oes cleddyf gyda fe?"

"Dw i ddim yn gwybod," meddai Mali. "Mae'r clogyn yn fawr ac yn dywyll."

Mae Mali'n edrych ar y gannwyll, ac mae hi'n siarad yn dawel.

"Ddoe, penhwyad. Neithiwr, draig yn y gegin. A heddiw, dieithryn."

Mae Mali'n codi'r bluen eto, ac mae hi'n ysgrifennu un cwestiwn yn y dyddiadur: Pwy yw'r dieithryn?

"Sut wyt ti'n teimlo, Mali?" meddai Arth.

"Dw i'n teimlo'n oer," meddai Mali. "Paid ag anghofio, Arth: mae'r dyddiadur yn gyfrinachol."

"Dw i ddim yn flinedig nawr," meddai Arth yn dawel.

"Wyt ti'n ofni, Arth?" meddai Mali.

"Nac ydw," meddai Arth. "Wel… ydw."

"A fi hefyd," meddai Mali.

Ond mae Dafi'n cysgu wrth y ffwrn, ac yn sydyn mae e'n tisian: "Atishŵ!" Dyw'r gannwyll ddim yn llosgi nawr, ac mae'r gegin yn dywyll.

Mae Arth yn edrych mas ar y ffordd dywyll, ond dyw e ddim yn gweld dim byd: dim ceffyl, dim dieithryn.

Nodyn (Saesneg)

Mali's diary tells what happened at a past time, one event after another. For this Welsh uses a past tense: a verb form for a finished event in the past, like English 'I went' or 'I saw'. The diary's commonest way to make it is Wnes i ('I did') followed by a verb-noun, the dictionary form of a verb: Wnes i weld llaw fawr Myrddin ('I saw Myrddin's big hand', literally 'I did see'). Wnes i comes from gwneud ('to do, to make'): wnes is the soft-mutated form of gwnes (the g- drops, as in gweld → weld), and spoken Welsh commonly uses it in statements as well as questions. For ti ('you') the form is Wnest ti: Wnest ti weld y penhwyad ('You saw the pike').

The verb-noun after wnes i and wnest ti takes the soft mutation, the same softening of the first sound as after dy ('your') in Pennod 10: pysgota becomes wnes i bysgota ('I fished'), cuddio becomes wnes i guddio ('I hid'), teimlo becomes Wnes i deimlo'n oer ('I felt cold'), and gweld loses its g- in wnes i weld ('I saw'). Words beginning with a sound that the soft mutation does not touch stay as they are: Wnes i nofio ('I swam'), Wnes i eistedd ('I sat'), wnes i chwerthin ('I laughed'), wnes i ffeindio ('I found'). Unlike after wedi (Pennod 11), the verb-noun changes here. Wnes i softens only the verb-noun after it, not that verb-noun's object as well: wnes i weld llaw fawr Myrddin keeps llaw ('hand').

A question uses the same words with a rising voice and, in writing, a question mark: Wnest ti ateb y cwestiwn? ('Did you answer the question?'). Mali answers with a full sentence: Wnes i ateb y dieithryn ('I answered the stranger'). To ask what someone did, say Beth wnest ti? ('What did you do?'), as Arth does twice: Beth wnest ti ddoe, Mali? ('What did you do yesterday, Mali?') and Beth wnest ti heddiw? ('What did you do today?'). No verb-noun follows here, because wnest ti itself means 'you did'.

Three common verbs also have short past forms of their own, and this chapter uses them: es i ('I went', from mynd), des i ('I came', from dod) and ces i ('I had, I got', from cael). Yn gyntaf, es i i'r afon ('First, I went to the river'); des i i'r llys ('I came to the court'); neithiwr ces i gawl ('last night I had cawl').

The diary also has a second kind of past, where the verb itself carries an ending: -ais i for 'I'. Gwelais i ('I saw', from gweld) and clywais i ('I heard', from clywed) work like this, and the margin glosses gwelais i = wnes i weld. For ti the ending is -aist ti, and at the start of a question the first sound softens: Welaist ti fy nghleddyf i? ('Did you see my sword?').

After a one-word past form such as ces i or gwelais i (not wnes i + verb-noun), a noun object (the thing seen or got) softens: ces i gawl ('I had cawl', from cawl), gwelais i benhwyad mawr ('I saw a big pike', from penhwyad), gwelais i ddyn rhyfedd ('I saw a strange man', from dyn). This object mutation does not pass through the article: gwelais i'r llanast ('I saw the mess'). The article keeps its own rules, though: a feminine singular noun still softens after it, as in cynna'r gannwyll ('light the candle', from cannwyll).

Wedi or wnes i? Both talk about the past, but in different ways. Dw i wedi … (Pennod 11) links a finished action to the present: Dw i wedi anghofio'r bont ('I've forgotten the bridge'; it is gone from Arth's head now). Wnes i … tells an event as a step in a story: Wnes i guddio dan y bont ('I hid under the bridge'). No time word decides the choice: heddiw ('today') appears with both, in Wyt ti wedi ysgrifennu heddiw? ('Have you written today?') and Beth wnest ti heddiw? ('What did you do today?').

The diary puts its events in order with yn gyntaf ('first'), wedyn ('afterwards, then') and yn olaf ('finally').

Remaining reference translations: Wnes i bysgota gydag Arth means “I fished with Arth”; Mae’r cleddyf yn y neuadd means “The sword is in the hall”; Dw i wedi ysgrifennu heddiw yn barod means “I have already written today”. Dw i’n pysgota and Dw i’n cuddio mean “I am fishing” and “I am hiding”; Dw i’n nofio, Dw i’n ateb and Dw i’n chwerthin mean “I am swimming”, “I am answering” and “I am laughing”.

Reference translations: Dw i’n gweld (nawr) — “I see / am seeing (now)”; Dw i’n teimlo’n oer — “I feel cold”; wnest ti nofio — “you swam”.

Rhan 2 · Pennod 13

Hedfanodd Arth

I. Hedfanodd Arth

Un bore, daeth Myrddin i'r buarth gyda Mali ac Arth. Edrychodd e ar yr awyr las, ac edrychodd e ar Arth.

dod → des i → daeth e · Mae e'n edrych → edrychodd e

"Wyt ti eisiau hedfan, Arth?" meddai Myrddin.

"Ydw!" meddai Arth. "Gyda'r adar?"

"Gyda'r adar," meddai Myrddin, a gwenodd e.

"A fi?" meddai Mali. "Dw i eisiau hedfan hefyd!"

"Dim heddiw, Mali," meddai Myrddin. "Heddiw, mae gwaith gyda ti: edrych ar yr awyr, ac edrych ar Arth."

Cododd Myrddin ei law. Yn sydyn, trodd Arth yn hebog: aderyn bach llwyd, gyda llygaid melyn.

troi → trodd: bachgen → hebog · hebog

"Arth!" meddai Mali. "Rwyt ti'n hebog go iawn!"

Edrychodd Arth ar ei adenydd: adenydd llwyd, hir. Edrychodd e ar ei gorff e: dim cen, dim esgyll nawr, ond plu llwyd ar ei gefn e!

adain, adenydd

"Ble mae fy nwylo i?" meddai e.

"Does dim dwylo gyda ti, Arth," meddai Mali. "Mae adenydd gyda ti! Edrych ar dy adenydd di!"

Yn gyntaf, cododd Arth ei adenydd. Wedyn hedfanodd e i fyny, i fyny, i'r awyr las.

i fyny = ↑ · ddoe ↔ nawr

"Hedfanodd Arth!" meddai Mali yn dawel.

Hedfanodd Arth uwchben y llys. Gwelodd e Cai yn y buarth, gyda'r cleddyf a'r darian. Gwelodd e Modlen yn y drws, a Dafi ar y to. Gwelodd e'r to mawr ar y neuadd, a Pero'n cysgu wrth y stabl, wrth gwrs. Gwelodd e Elen yn yr ardd, a Cynyr gyda'r ceffylau.

uwchben ↔ dan · gweld → gwelais i → gwelodd e · gwelodd e'r to ↔ gwelodd e gysgod

Ond edrychodd Dafi i fyny ar yr hebog, ac yn sydyn daeth tân bach o'i geg e!

"Dafi!" meddai Modlen o'r drws, gyda'r llwy bren yn ei llaw hi. "Paid â llosgi'r to!"

"Dafi, paid ag ofni!" meddai Arth. "Arth dw i!"

"Arth? Hebog!" meddai Dafi. "Dafi'n ofni hebog!"

"Arth! Paid â chwarae gyda Dafi!" meddai Mali o'r buarth, ac edrychodd hi i fyny.

"Mae'r llys yn fach iawn!" meddai Arth.

Hedfanodd e i'r cymylau gwyn. Gwelodd e olau'r haul ar y cymylau, ac wedyn edrychodd e i lawr ar y cwm.

cwmwl, cymylau · cymylau cwmwl: dŵr yn yr awyr · gwelodd e olau ← golau · i lawr ↔ i fyny

"Mae golau'r haul yn gynnes ar fy adenydd i!" meddai Arth.

Hedfanodd e uwchben yr afon, y bont, y llyn a'r hen gwch.

"Dyma'r afon, dyma'r goedwig, a dyma'r llys bach!" meddai Arth. "Mae Cwm Helyg yn wahanol o'r awyr: map yw e!"

yn wahanol ← gwahanol

Wedyn gwelodd e gysgod bach ar y maes: cysgod hebog! A gwelodd e lygoden fach ar y maes, wrth y cysgod.

gwelodd e gysgod ← cysgod · gwelodd e lygoden ← llygoden (b.)

Yn sydyn, disgynnodd Arth yn gyflym, gyflym i'r maes. Glaniodd e ar y maes, wrth y llygoden.

disgynnodd disgyn: mynd i lawr · Glaniodd glanio: awyr → maes

"Nage!" meddai Arth. "Dw i ddim yn bwyta llygod!"

Hedfanodd e i fyny eto, a rhedodd y llygoden i'r coed.

Wedyn hedfanodd e i'r goeden fawr, ac edrychodd e ar nyth bach: adar bach yn y nyth! Edrychodd yr adar bach ar Arth, ac yn sydyn cuddiodd yr adar eu pennau nhw yn y nyth.

nyth

"Dw i ddim yn benhwyad!" meddai Arth. "Arth dw i!"

Ond cuddiodd yr adar bach eto, ac aeth Arth i'r bryn yn dawel. Cyrhaeddodd e'r ogof dywyll ar y bryn uchel. Daeth gwynt oer, oer o'r ogof. Edrychodd Arth yn yr ogof ddwfn: cysgod, cysgod du, a dim byd. Wedyn gadawodd e'r bryn yn gyflym iawn.

mynd → es i → aeth e · Cyrhaeddodd = Daeth e i · gadawodd gadael ↔ cyrraedd

II. Y milwyr

Hedfanodd Arth uwchben y ffordd i'r dref. Gwelodd e filwyr ar y ffordd. Gwelodd e faner fawr hefyd, a draig goch ar y faner. Daeth y milwyr i lawr y ffordd yn araf.

gwelodd e filwyr ← milwyr (milwr) · faner · y faner ← baner (b.)

"Milwyr!" meddai Arth. "Pwy yw'r milwyr? Ble maen nhw'n mynd?" Gwelodd Arth y dieithryn hefyd, ar geffyl du, gyda'r milwyr.

ar geffyl ← ceffyl

"Y dieithryn!" meddai Arth. "Dyn rhyfedd Mali!"

Disgynnodd Arth yn agos, yn dawel, yn araf. Cyrhaeddodd y milwyr y bont, ac aeth y ceffylau i'r dŵr. Yn sydyn, cododd y dieithryn ei ben, ac edrychodd e ar yr hebog. Gwelodd Arth ei lygaid e: llygaid tywyll iawn.

"Hebog?" meddai'r dieithryn yn dawel. "Hebog Llys Cynyr?"

Trodd Arth, a hedfanodd e i'r llys yn gyflym, gyflym. Cyrhaeddodd e'r llys, ac edrychodd e ar y ffordd eto. Gadawodd y milwyr y bont, ac aeth y faner a'r ddraig goch i'r dref.

III. Hebog Cynyr

Glaniodd Arth ar wal y stabl, ac edrychodd e yn y stabl. Gwelodd e hen hebog yno, ar bren uchel.

ar bren ← pren

"Pwy wyt ti?" meddai'r hen hebog.

"Arth dw i," meddai Arth. "Bachgen dw i, ond heddiw hebog dw i."

"Hebog Cynyr dw i," meddai'r hen hebog. "Edrych ar fy nghoesau i: mae lledr ar fy nghoesau i." "Mae Cynyr yn clymu'r lledr wrth y pren."

lledr · clymu: lledr + pren → un

"Pam mae Cynyr yn clymu'r lledr?" meddai Arth.

"Fi yw hebog Cynyr," meddai'r hen aderyn. "Dw i'n byw yma: mae bwyd da gyda fi, ac mae'r stabl yn gynnes yn y nos." "Ond dw i ddim yn rhydd."

rhydd: dim lledr, dim clymu

"Ond mae'r awyr yn wych!" meddai Arth. "Y cymylau, yr haul, y golau…"

"Dw i'n cofio," meddai'r hen aderyn yn dawel.

"Wyt ti eisiau bod yn rhydd?" meddai Arth.

"Dw i'n hen, Arth," meddai'r hen aderyn. "Mae'r awyr yn fawr ac yn oer, ac mae'r stabl yn gynnes." "Ond rwyt ti'n wahanol: rwyt ti'n rhydd. Cer!"

wahanol ← gwahanol

Cododd Arth ei adenydd, ond edrychodd e ar yr hen aderyn eto, ac ar y lledr. Yn olaf, gadawodd e'r stabl, a hedfanodd e i'r buarth.

IV. Welaist ti'r ogof?

Edrychodd Mali i fyny ar yr awyr las yn y buarth, a gwenodd hi. Disgynnodd Arth i lawr i'r buarth, a glaniodd e wrth Myrddin a Mali.

"Croeso, hebog bach!" meddai Mali.

Gwnaeth Myrddin hud eto, ac yn sydyn trodd Arth yn fachgen.

gwneud → wnes i → gwnaeth e

"Arth! Welaist ti'r llys?" meddai Mali.

"Do!" meddai Arth. "Cai a Pero, a Dafi ar y to!" "Ac mae'r llys yn wahanol nawr: mae e'n fawr eto!"

Welaist ti …? → Do. / Naddo.

Nodyn (Saesneg)

This chapter tells its story in the simple past (the preterite): the verb form that reports a finished event, such as 'he flew'. Welsh makes it by adding an ending to the verb itself. Many regular verbs in this chapter use -odd for he and she: Mae Arth yn hedfan ('Arth is flying') becomes Hedfanodd Arth ('Arth flew'). The same form serves for e ('he') and hi ('she'): gwenodd e ('he smiled'), gwenodd hi ('she smiled').

The ending goes on the stem: the verb-noun (the dictionary form, used after yn) with its own ending taken off. Often that ending is a final vowel: codi → cododd ('raised'), glanio → glaniodd ('landed'), gwenu → gwenodd, cuddio → cuddiodd ('hid'). Edrych and hedfan add -odd to the whole word: edrychodd ('looked'), hedfanodd ('flew'). Others change more and are best learnt as you meet them: gweld → gwelodd ('saw'), rhedeg → rhedodd ('ran'), disgyn → disgynnodd ('dropped down'), troi → trodd ('turned'), cyrraedd → cyrhaeddodd ('reached'), gadael → gadawodd ('left').

In these sentences the verb comes first, then the subject (the one doing the action): Gwelodd e Cai yn y buarth ('He saw Cai in the yard'), Cododd Myrddin ei law ('Myrddin raised his hand'). With a noun subject the verb keeps this he/she form even when the noun is plural: Daeth y milwyr i lawr y ffordd ('The soldiers came down the road'), Cuddiodd yr adar bach eto ('The little birds hid again').

Four common verbs have irregular past forms, which have to be learnt. Mynd ('to go') gives aeth: aeth Arth i'r bryn ('Arth went to the hill'). Dod ('to come') gives daeth: Daeth Myrddin i'r buarth ('Myrddin came to the yard'). Cael ('to get, to have') gives cafodd: cafodd Arth gawl ('Arth had soup'). Gwneud ('to do, to make') gives gwnaeth: Gwnaeth Myrddin hud eto ('Myrddin did magic again'). The second table sets them beside the I-forms of Pennod 12 (es i 'I went', des i 'I came', ces i 'I got', wnes i 'I did', gwelais i 'I saw').

The object is the person or thing that the verb acts on. After an inflected verb (a verb with its own ending, like gwelodd) and its subject, a noun object takes the soft mutation, the softening of a word's first sound: gwelodd e filwyr ('he saw soldiers', from milwyr), Gwelodd e faner fawr ('He saw a big banner', from baner), gwelodd e gysgod bach ('he saw a little shadow', from cysgod), cafodd Arth gawl (from cawl). Here ll softens as well: gwelodd e lygoden fach ('he saw a little mouse', from llygoden). The ll- and rh- exception belongs only to certain triggers, such as yn before a description. The verb-triggered mutation does not pass through y/'r; the article still follows its usual feminine-singular mutation rule: gwelodd e'r to mawr ('he saw the big roof'). In this course, personal names are left unmutated: Gwelodd e Modlen yn y drws ('He saw Modlen in the doorway').

In a question the inflected verb's own first sound softens too: Welaist ti'r ogof? ('Did you see the cave?', from gwelaist ti), Gest ti lygoden? ('Did you get a mouse?', from cest ti). Wnest ti …? from Pennod 12 works the same way: Wnest ti fwyta'r adar bach? ('Did you eat the little birds?'). Pensum C asks about Arth like this: Beth welodd Arth ar y ffordd? ('What did Arth see on the road?').

Welsh usually answers a yes/no question by echoing its verb: Wyt ti'n flinedig? Ydw ('Are you tired? Yes, I am'). A question in the simple past is answered instead with Do ('yes') or Naddo ('no'): Welaist ti'r llys? Do! ('Did you see the court? Yes!'), Gest ti lygoden? Naddo! ('Did you get a mouse? No!').

Both the -odd form and wedi (Pennod 11) speak of the past. Hedfanodd Arth tells what happened, one event after another, the way this story is told. Mae e wedi hedfan ('He has flown'), in the time-line diagram, looks back from the present at something that has happened, as when Cai asks Ble wyt ti wedi bod? ('Where have you been?') and Arth answers Dw i wedi bod yn hebog! ('I've been a hawk!').

Complete table examples: Mae Arth yn hedfan — “Arth is flying”; Hedfanodd Arth i fyny — “Arth flew up”; Mae e’n gweld milwyr — “He sees soldiers”; Gwelodd e filwyr ar y ffordd — “He saw soldiers on the road”; Mae e’n glanio — “He is landing”; Glaniodd e ar y maes — “He landed in the field”; Mae Myrddin yn codi ei law — “Myrddin is raising his hand”; Cododd Myrddin ei law — “Myrddin raised his hand”; Mae Arth yn troi’n hebog — “Arth is turning into a hawk”; Trodd Arth yn hebog — “Arth turned into a hawk”; gwelodd e’r ogof — “he saw the cave”; gwelodd e’r cysgod — “he saw the shadow”. Gwelodd e gysgod, filwyr, lygoden, faner gives the changed forms in “he saw a shadow, soldiers, a mouse, a flag”; the listed base forms are cysgod, milwyr, llygoden, baner.

Rhan 2 · Pennod 14

Yn y ffair

I. I'r ffair

Mae hi'n fore, ac mae'r haul yn gynnes: does dim cymylau heddiw. Heddiw mae ffair yn y dref, ac mae Elen, Modlen, Mali ac Arth yn mynd i'r ffair. Mae Cynyr a Cai'n aros yn y llys, ac mae Pero'n cysgu wrth y stabl.

"Dw i eisiau gweld y ffair!" meddai Arth, ac mae e'n rhedeg ar y ffordd.

"Paid â rhedeg, Arth!" meddai Modlen. "Mae wyau yn y fasged!"

"Dw i ddim eisiau gweld y dieithryn," meddai Arth.

Mae basged fawr gyda Modlen.

"Wyau!" meddai Modlen, ac mae hi'n edrych yn y fasged ac yn cyfrif yr wyau. "Un, dau, tri, pedwar, pump, chwech, saith, wyth, naw, deg! Deg wy."

"Dafi," meddai Mali yn dawel. "Mae e eisiau gweld y ffair."

Mae Elen yn edrych ar y mwg hefyd.

"Oes rhywbeth yn y fasged, Mali?" meddai hi.

"Oes, Mam," meddai Mali. "Caws."

Mae Elen yn gwenu, ond dyw hi ddim yn siarad.

Maen nhw'n cyrraedd y ffair ar y maes wrth y dref. Mae'r ffair yn fawr ac yn brysur, ac mae dynion a menywod yn prynu ac yn gwerthu. Mae hebog yma hefyd, gyda lledr ar ei goesau ac adenydd llwyd. Mae dyn yn gwerthu pedwar mochyn, ac mae menyw'n gwerthu pedair dafad a buwch fawr.

III. Y gwlân

Wedyn mae Modlen yn prynu cig i'r cawl, blawd i'r bara, a jwg newydd: mae'r hen jwg wedi torri. Mae Modlen yn hapus iawn.

"Dafi, rwyt ti'n ddrwg iawn!" meddai Mali yn dawel.

V. Y dieithryn

Nawr mae'r haul yn mynd i lawr, mae'r toeau'n goch, ac mae'r ffair yn dawel. Mae tŷ mawr yn y dref, ac mae dynion yn bwyta ac yn yfed yno: tŷ'r tafarnwr yw e. Mae baner fawr gyda draig goch ar y wal, ac mae ceffyl mawr du wrth y drws.

Wedyn mae Modlen yn galw o'r ffordd: "Arth! Mali! Dewch!"

Nodyn (Saesneg)

This chapter counts. The numbers from one to ten are un, dau, tri, pedwar, pump, chwech, saith, wyth, naw, deg, as Modlen counts her eggs, and ugain is twenty: Ugain ceiniog ('Twenty pennies'). Eleven is un ar ddeg, already met in the age phrase of Pennod 8: bachgen un ar ddeg oed ('an eleven-year-old boy').

In the direct number + noun pattern shown here, Welsh uses the singular noun, not the plural: deg wy ('ten eggs', not wyau), naw afal ('nine apples'), saith ceiniog ('seven pennies'), deg bachgen ('ten boys'). When referring to several eggs, pennies or apples without a numeral, use their plural forms: yr wyau ('the eggs'), y ceiniogau ('the pennies'), yr afalau ('the apples'). A number can also stand alone when the noun is clear: Mae Elen yn rhoi dwy geiniog i Arth, a dwy i Mali ('Elen gives two pennies to Arth, and two to Mali').

Every Welsh noun is either masculine or feminine; the vocabulary marks them (g.) and (b.). Two, three and four have a separate feminine form, used with feminine nouns: dau afal ('two apples') but dwy geiniog ('two pennies'), tri chaws ('three cheeses') but tair ceiniog ('three pennies'), pedwar mochyn ('four pigs') but pedair dafad ('four sheep'). In this chapter ceiniog ('penny'), dafad ('sheep') and buwch ('cow') are feminine; afal ('apple'), wy ('egg'), caws ('cheese') and mochyn ('pig') are masculine. The other numbers have one form for both genders, though un treats them differently, as below.

Some numbers change the first sound of the next word. Un ('one') gives a feminine singular noun the soft mutation, the softening of a word's first sound met after yn and y: un geiniog ('one penny', from ceiniog). A masculine noun stays as it is: un bachgen ('one boy'). As after yn, a feminine noun beginning with ll- or rh- does not soften after un. Dau and dwy soften the noun after them: dau gaws ('two cheeses', from caws), dwy geiniog ('two pennies'). Tair and pedair do not: tair ceiniog, pedair ceiniog.

Tri and chwe cause the aspirate mutation, which changes only c, p and t (to ch, ph and th): tri chaws ('three cheeses', from caws), chwe cheiniog ('six pennies', from ceiniog). The story shows only c → ch. A word beginning with any other sound stays as it is: tri afal ('three apples').

When counting, five and six are pump and chwech. Before a noun they shorten to pum and chwe: pum ceiniog ('five pennies'), chwe cheiniog ('six pennies'). Mali adds up the wool like this: Tair ceiniog a dwy geiniog: pum ceiniog, dim saith! ('Three pennies and two pennies: five pennies, not seven!').

A number can itself be softened by the word before it, like any other word. After dyma: Dyma dair ceiniog ('Here are three pennies', from tair). As the thing asked for after Gaf i: Gaf i ddau afal? ('May I have two apples?', from dau).

Faint yw …? asks a price: Faint yw'r caws? ('How much is the cheese?') Tair ceiniog ('Three pennies'). Faint yw'r mochyn bach? ('How much is the little pig?') Ugain ceiniog ('Twenty pennies'). As the examples show, the answer can be just the amount.

Gaf i …? ('May I have …?') asks for something. It is a question form of cael ('to get, to have'), with its first sound softened, like Gest ti …? in Pennod 13. The answers are Cei ('Yes, you may') and Na chei ('No, you may not'), where na changes the c of cei to ch: Gaf i afal? Cei ('May I have an apple? Yes'); Modlen, gaf i fochyn bach? Na chei! ('Modlen, may I have a little pig? No!'). The thing asked for is the object, so it softens as objects did in Pennod 13: fochyn from mochyn, ddau from dau.

Nodyn (Saesneg)

A demonstrative is a pointing word, like 'this' and 'that'. Welsh chooses its demonstrative by asking two questions. Is the thing near (yma, 'here') or further off (yno, 'there')? And is the noun masculine or feminine? (Every Welsh noun is one or the other; the vocabulary marks it (g.) for masculine or (b.) for feminine.)

Standing alone, 'this one' is hwn for a masculine thing and hon for a feminine one. Cai holds up something small and white and asks Beth yw hwn? ('What is this?'). Mali names it, and because pluen ('feather') is feminine she says hon: Pluen yw hon, Cai ('This is a feather, Cai'). The watch, oriawr, is feminine too: Beth yw hon? ('What is this?'), Ydy hon yn agor y bocs? ('Does this one open the box?'). For 'that one', further off, say hwnnw (masculine) or honno (feminine): Beth yw hwnnw? ('What is that?'), about the umbrella in the cupboard; Ymbarél yw hwnnw ('That is an umbrella'); Llwy yw honno ('That is a spoon'). The order is the X yw Y order of earlier chapters: the name of the thing, then yw, then the pointing word. When Arth finds the key, Dafi asks from the shadow Ydy hwn yn agor y bocs? ('Does this open the box?'), and Mali corrects him, Hon, Dafi: allwedd yw hi ('Hon, not hwn, Dafi: it's a key'), because allwedd ('key') is feminine. The words e ('he, it') and hi ('she, it') follow the same gender for things: the watch is hi, Mae hi'n dangos yr amser ('It shows the time'), and the umbrella is e, Mae e'n ddefnyddiol iawn ('It is very useful').

With a noun, put y (yr, 'r: 'the') before the noun and yma ('this') or yna ('that') after it. Arth holds up the wheel: Ydy'r olwyn yma'n agor y bocs? ('Does this wheel open the box?'). Cai looks at the button: Ydy'r botwm yna'n ddefnyddiol? ('Is that button useful?'). After his fall he says Dw i ddim yn hoffi'r ymbarél yna ('I don't like that umbrella'). Yma and yna stay the same for both genders. Honno can follow a noun in the same place: the story's last paragraph opens Y noson honno ('That night'; noson is feminine). Keep yna ('that', after a noun) apart from yno ('there'): Mae tri pheth yno hefyd ('There are three things there too'). In tri pheth, peth ('thing') changes to pheth after tri ('three'), the Pennod 14 rule.

For several things, 'these (ones)' standing alone is y rhain, for either gender: Edrych ar y rhain! ('Look at these!'), Dyw'r rhain ddim yn allweddi, blant ('These aren't keys, children'). After a plural noun (one meaning more than one), 'these' is hyn and 'those' is hynny: y pethau hyn ('these things'; pethau is the plural of peth), A'r pethau hynny, i fyny ar y silff? ('And those things, up on the shelf?'). As the margin note at the first one says, y pethau yma means the same as y pethau hyn.

Hyn and hynny have a second use, with no noun at all. In this chapter, hwn and hon identify individual objects, while hyn and hynny refer to Mali's experience or to something just said. Looking through the spectacles, Mali says Mae hyn yn rhyfedd! ('This is strange!'); after the vision she asks Beth yw hyn, Myrddin? ('What is this, Myrddin?'). Hynny points back at what someone has said: Dw i ddim yn deall hynny ('I don't understand that'), Dw i ddim yn credu hynny! ('I don't believe that!').

Dyna is the partner of dyma ('here is'), which you already know: dyma points at something near, and dyna at something further off or just found ('there is, that's'). Like dyma, dyna gives a following noun the soft mutation, a softening of its first sound: Dyna farchog! ('There's a knight!', from marchog), Dyna fachgen gyda gwallt coch ('That's a boy with red hair', from bachgen), as in Dyma lyfr ('Here's a book', from llyfr, Pennod 8). When the article intervenes, dyna causes no additional mutation; the article's own feminine-singular mutation rule still applies: Dyna'r allwedd! ('There's the key!'), like Dyma'r bwrdd hir ('Here's the long table', Pennod 6). Myrddin's Dyna hi! ('There it is!') uses hi because allwedd is feminine.
